items.en: F-Zero X on 3DS — Old and New, native, with the 64DD Expansion Kit

A post-mortem of porting G-Diffuser, the F-Zero X decompilation, to the Nintendo 3DS — v1.0.0, covering both the original 24-day sprint that put it on a New 3DS at 60 fps in 3D (2026-08-11 to 09-03) and the 43-day second phase that added Old 3DS support, a native renderer, and the Expansion Kit (2026-09-07 to 10-19). One person directed throughout; one long-lived Claude session orchestrated; 147 subagents built the first phase and many more carried the second.
The console went from a black screen to a native-60 stereoscopic racer, then from a New-3DS-only build to a four-way release covering both consoles with and without the 64DD expansion.
The clips and photos below are from v0.9 (2026-09), before DASH replaced the debug console on the bottom screen.

Three released console builds from one source tree, all booting from the HOME menu (.cia) or the homebrew launcher (.3dsx): the base game for Old 3DS / 2DS and for New 3DS / New 2DS XL, and a New 3DS build with the 64DD Expansion Kit (course editor and machine creator, playable with a user-supplied disk image). Every build reads prebaked asset archives from the SD card — no ROM or disk image ever ships with the game.

They play the whole game: Grand Prix, Time Trial, Practice, Death Race, and the machine editor screens, with music and effects on the real DSP, stereoscopic 3D on the slider, a bottom-screen dashboard with three HUD layouts and an idle view outside races, and clean HOME suspend, resume, close, lid sleep and power-off. The New 3DS build keeps the native-60 frame pacing the first phase reached; the Old 3DS build gets to a comparable result by a different route. At v1.0.0, with no ini, both builds default to that same route: the native renderer ([perf] preset = auto). The New 3DS's first-phase render-thread/per-draw-stereo path is still built in and reachable with an explicit ini, but is no longer the default — see Frontier and Pushing the boundaries for the two builds compared side by side.
- decomp: the F-Zero X decompilation (inspectredc/fzerox), untouched upstream, plus a patch stack.
- libultraship: the N64 runtime (Kenix3), untouched upstream, including a 13-line newlib fix that lets it build on devkitARM; it still draws every menu and non-race screen.
- port/3ds: 15,039 lines as of the first phase, since grown: a citro3d rendering backend, stereo, audio, input, menu, lifecycle, render thread, profilers, packaging.

- the native renderer (added in the second phase): an owned interpreter that skips the per-frame display-list walk for race geometry, and is the v1.0.0 default on both consoles — see Frontier for how, and why it is what lets the Old 3DS keep up.
The headline numbers on hardware, first phase (New 3DS)
- 08-11 → 08-14: from research to a race. Feasibility dossier, plan for a team of agents, five parallel foundation streams, six boot bugs, first race at 12–20 fps in the emulator.

- 08-20 → 08-22: from pink to playable, then to a real console. Fog, HUD, livery, shadow, sky fixed; the loadblock discovery took menus from 27 to 60 fps; first hardware run 08-21 ("wow it runs amazing"); audio the same evening.
- 08-27 → 08-28: product grade. Five-agent fleet drop, stereo armed, touch menu, rival detail, GPU vertex-transform moonshot built and shelved, README with legal notice, release package.

- 09-01 → 09-02: lifecycle and the last big lever. HOME crash and close-from-HOME hang fixed; a bridge output cache proven a NO-GO and replaced by memoizing each sub-display-list's classification instead of re-scanning it every frame; LOCKED-60 campaign launched with four parallel levers.

- 09-02 → 09-03: multi-core. Render thread on core 2, one-frame-ahead mode, bridge on main, auto LOD; median 59.6 with 53% of frames at cap; crash fixed; viewport placement fixed; stereo markers anchored.
Not originally planned; it ran 09-07 to 10-19, 43 calendar days.

- 09-07 → 09-29: scoping, then making it fit. The Old 3DS milestone, previously written off, was restarted; parallel agents fit the build into its 64 MB app region (the RDRAM arena halved, audio streamed instead of resident, texture uploads capped); on 2026-09-29, in the first hardware session on a real Old 3DS, the shipped (New-3DS-era, 16 MiB RDRAM) build died at boot while the -DGDX_3DS_O3DS=ON profile, built to fit the console's memory grant, booted and raced the same session at about 10 fps.

- 09-29 → 09-30: finding the real costs. A narrowed audio lock cut the race-wall wait on the Old 3DS by about 20 ms a frame; frame skipping ended the game's accidental slow motion; a first retained-mode renderer won big in the emulator and barely moved the number on hardware.

- 09-30 → 10-01: the probe that changed the plan. Hardware performance counters showed the real limit was instruction-cache misses, not instruction count. A pose-replay fallback was built and worked, then was set aside on the user's call: "we should go for a real 60! i still believe it has to be possible."

- 10-01 → 10-02: the native renderer. Rebuilt around the cache instead of around instruction counts, one small loop per race category, sized to fit the 16 KB instruction cache. Median frame time on a 2D Grand Prix race reached 16.5 ms.

- 10-03 → 10-08: 3D at 60, on the Old 3DS too. A per-eye resubmit with its own swap-pacing mode reached 59–60 fps in 3D on most Grand Prix courses; the heaviest courses (Silence, Sand Ocean) can still trip the frame-skip safety net to a steady 30 fps mid-race.

- 10-08 → 10-19: the Expansion Kit, a dashboard, and release. The 64DD Expansion Kit verified tick-for-tick identical under the native renderer and booted on the Old 3DS, which then proved too slow to release it on; the bottom-screen DASH shipped; a standing adversarial review audited the merged result before the v1.0.0 release.
See Agentic workflow for how the second phase was run and Old 3DS for the full campaign, card by card.

Three months after Elon Musk declared that Grok would release a full-length, “historically accurate” movie version of “The Odyssey,” Grok has published a whole seven minutes — what the company is now calling “Episode 1 of our Odyssey series.”

Musk had previously lashed out at Christopher Nolan’s version of “The Odyssey” because Nolan cast nonwhite and transgender actors. And Nolan is, in many ways, a perfect foil for Musk — while SpaceX and Tesla CEO hypes up data centers in space and posts an unending stream of AI-generated content, Nolan has described himself as “a techno-skeptic” and said that before AI, he’d never seen a technology “so completely rejected by the public.”

And while Nolan’s version of “The Odyssey” certainly used plenty of visual effects, it’s primarily a feat of practical filmmaking, with a shoot spanning six countries and a cast and crew of thousands. After its release in July, the film became an extraordinary box office success, selling out Imax screenings for months and becoming the likely front-runner at the next Academy Awards.
As for the Grok version of “The Odyssey” (created in collaboration with Wonder Studios and director Dev Walker), well, you can watch for yourself.

I’ll admit it’s not as spectacularly ugly as I’d expected, and certainly more impressive than other videos that Musk has posted recently. If I didn’t know better, there were moments when I might have thought these were real actors sailing across a real sea. And while I can’t speak to Grok’s historical accuracy, it does seem that all the characters come in a Musk-approved skin color, while the narrator uses a British accent that will sound familiar to anyone who’s played a fantasy video game or watched a generic Hollywood epic from the past 25 years.

What the footage really lacks is any sense of artistry, inspiration, or human interest. The backstory — delivered via the aforementioned voiceover — seems to go on forever, finally giving way to one bearded face after another, each shouting stilted lines that make Nolan’s dialogue sound like Shakespeare.

While a few individual shots might provide a reasonable simulacrum of reality, the whole thing feels completely airless, offering viewers no sense of momentum, no reason to care about anyone or anything on-screen. And where I had no trouble paying attention for the nearly three-hour runtime of Nolan’s “Odyssey,” I was listlessly checking how much I had left before the Grok version was even halfway through.
It’s hard to imagine being interested in another seven minutes of this, much less a full movie’s worth.

A scalable AI system requires a strong foundation. Data, engineering, platforms, operating models, and governance must converge to work as one. This session from MIT Technology Review's EmTech Future conference explores what it takes to build that foundation in a highly regulated environment and how a responsible, trustworthy implementation can turn emerging capabilities, including agentic systems, into lasting value for investors.
Jing Wang, Principal, Center for AI and Insights, Vanguard

Jing Wang leads Vanguard's Center for AI & Insights (CAI), advancing the firm's AI, machine learning, generative AI, and behavioral science capabilities. Her team drives enterprise-wide innovation, research, and delivery, enabling Vanguard to translate emerging technologies into trusted solutions that enhance client experiences, improve investor outcomes, and create measurable business value.

Before her current position, Jing served in a range of leadership roles across Vanguard's Financial Services, Workplace Solutions, International, and Corporate Services divisions. Throughout her tenure, she has led teams and enterprise initiatives that advanced strategic priorities, strengthened client outcomes, and drove business performance across the firm.

She joined Vanguard in 2009 after several years as a Principal at the Boston Consulting Group. Jing earned a B.S. in Physics from the University of Science and Technology of China, a Ph.D. from the University of Pennsylvania, and an M.B.A. in Finance and Marketing from the Wharton School of Business at the University of Pennsylvania. Jing holds Series 7, 24, and 65 licenses.

9:10 a.m. I keep my phone on Do Not Disturb for two hours as I drink coffee, burn palo santo, and finish Play It As It Lays. I’ve been separated for over a year. We get into a discussion about how he has a crush on me, is embarrassed other dancers know him, and only wants to spend time with me. He buys three more dances.

A downside: I am nocturnal and can’t settle into sleep right away. I watch Law & Order to bore myself into drifting off.
4:30 a.m. Send my friend a voice note recapping my night. I call these “Tales From the Strip.”

I tell him about the divorce being finalized and he congratulates me. My dad likes to hear news before my mom. It makes him feel special. (I immediately call my mom after.)
3:42 p.m. David texts confirming tomorrow night. He’s not drinking so will come right over. Efficient!

5 p.m. Two-hour dance workshop in the city. My body’s exhausted, but I commit to dancing for myself at least once a week. The instructor lends me a ball to roll out a major knot in my calf from wearing heels so much.

8 p.m. Walk to a bar with friends. I met the bartender a few weeks ago at the club. It was his birthday; we hit it off. He told me I should swing by sometime, so this is me swinging. This is the first time I’ve been open to meeting a guy out of the club. Call it a dancer’s intuition, but it’s easy to discern who has a strip-club addiction and who goes for a special occasion. I’d never date a strip-club regular.

8:15 p.m. We see Bartender Eric, who says hi. My friends and I quietly toast my divorce so Eric doesn’t overhear. He comps two rounds and shots. We chat and realize we live very close to each other. He asks me to dinner. I give him my number and real name.

9:30 p.m. My friends leave. Eric sits on the barstool next to mine and holds my hand, asking what music I like and where I grew up. I’m at risk of kissing him at his workplace, so it’s time to go. Outside, we hug in front of his smoking co-workers.

10 p.m. Home posting my workshop videos to Stories. I dislike social media, but it’s important to stay connected to my dance community. I don’t let men follow me until we sleep together. I’ve had lurkers who never text me but instantly watch Stories of me dancing — ew.

10:30 p.m. Eric texts proposing a restaurant and time. He’ll walk to pick me up, then we’ll take a car to dinner. Maybe this will go somewhere. I haven’t had a second date in months, which is damaging my self-confidence. I can’t blame my looks … The issue must boil down to my personality.
10:10 a.m. Mark sends a photo of the book he’s reading. Decide to make him wait. Texting back inconsistently makes him respond faster.

2:45 p.m. Walk to the local diner with just-okay food. Order a veggie burger with cheese, fries, coffee, and a Bloody Mary. I could drink tomato juice all day. Read Lisa Taddeo’s Animal while I wait for my food, which is actually excellent today.

8:22 p.m. David arrives. He asks for a seltzer. I ask him to get in bed to warm me up. I keep my apartment cold but kept the windows open for too long today. Under my covers, he tells me about his week. Then a constant stream of kissing and touching. I’m on top, sliding his dick hot-dog-bunned between my ass cheeks. It’s sexy. I don’t question it. I love sex with David because there’s no judgment. Things get weird; we discover what feels good, then do it until our legs get too tired and we have to switch.

11:27 p.m. David and I have an unspoken mutual agreement that he doesn’t spend the night. I enjoy his company, but sleeping over’s too intimate. Before he leaves, I tell him I’ll miss him while he’s traveling, which is true.

11:30 p.m. I inhale everything in my fridge: a handful of shredded cheese, lemon-dill hummus, pretzels. Take magnesium and tuck myself in. It’s a new moon, and my astrology app told me to manifest what I want in relationships, so I try and figure that out before falling asleep.

10:24 a.m. I continue with Animal. It’s not lost on me that I’ve been reading a lot about sex workers. My next book is Larry McMurtry’s Lonesome Dove, recommended by several people, so I have high hopes. It’s nice to have something to look forward to.

1:55 p.m. Text my friends a draft of a message to Mark about him talking to other dancers. The tone is serious and sets boundaries (not my strength), but I think it’s too long and finger-wagging. They agree it’s not going to be effective. We brainstorm via voice notes. We conclude I should come across as flirty, not mention money, and keep trying to get him to come in to see me. I’m selling “fantasy girl who never gets annoyed” even though I’m consistently irked by men.

2:26 p.m. Instead of the workshopped text, I write Mark, “Since you showed me yours, I’ll show you mine,” with a photo of Animal. He replies right away saying he can’t wait to hear about it. Ugh. I’ll send the other text later.

4:30 p.m. Meet a friend for martinis and fries before we see Silence of the Lambs. We discuss the merits of dating an ugly man if he has money and is nice, then get into the different tiers of attractiveness. We settle on highest to lowest: gorgeous, sexy, hot, attractive, not ugly, ugly. We agree you never go for gorgeous but ideally land someone in the sexy-to-attractive range.

8:04 p.m. Walk to another bar after the movie. We smoke Chinese cigarettes and text our friend working a pop-up queer strip club about how it’s going. Conversation turns to how Pride & Prejudice (Keira Knightley version) and Silence of the Lambs are perfect movies. We laugh like maniacs over getting chills during P&P scenes we love. We both have obnoxious laughs — and we’re cheap laughs at that, so it becomes a cackle session.

It’s been two months since Donald Trump changed the name of a landmark, institution, or geographic feature, and he’s clearly itching to rebrand something. Earlier this week, the president renewed his call for New Mexico to “immediately change its name to New America” in a post on Truth Social:

As we learned when Trump first raised the idea in early September, this isn’t actually going to happen. The president has the power to direct federal agencies to use names like the “Gulf of America” and “Lake America.” And he successfully bullied tech executives into making those changes in their map apps, too. But he can’t simply inform a state that it now has an entirely different name. As the New York Times noted, he has no legal authority to do so, and in this case the state constitution says, “The name of this state is New Mexico,” before laying out its boundaries.

At a Wednesday-night rally in South Carolina, Trump suggested he’d moved on and was looking for other things to rename. He revealed he’d called up Sundar Pichai and floated the idea of renaming the Atlantic Ocean, but the Google CEO talked him out of it.
“I only like two oceans: the Atlantic Ocean and the Pacific Ocean,” the president said. “I’m not gonna put either ‘Trump’ or ‘America’ on any other ocean but these two.”

Trump continued, “So we seriously looked at the Atlantic Ocean. And I called Google Maps, who are really great with the lake. And I spoke to a brilliant guy, Sundar, he heads all of Google … You know they’re still rattled from the gulf. And I said, ‘Sundar, I’m thinking of the Atlantic Ocean. Could you handle it?’”
He said Pichai answered, “No, no, this time, I’m not doing it. Oceans are different, sir. They cover really a lot of countries. Please don’t ask us to do that.”
So, Trump concluded, he’d “probably pass” on renaming the Atlantic. But then he added, “Pacific Ocean, we’re gonna call it the American Ocean,” before weaving away to other topics.

Trump made a quip about renaming the Atlantic or Pacific back in August. It’s always hard to tell if he’s serious about his idiotic renaming proposals or just trolling. But it seemed like the latter after Trump told the Pichai anecdote again at a rally in Iowa on Thursday night.

“I called up Sundar. I got the lake, and I got the gulf. I said, ‘Sundar’ — I was only kidding — ‘I’ve have a new one,’” Trump recalled. “I actually sent him a picture of the Atlantic Ocean called the ‘American Ocean,’ and he actually called me and said, ‘Sir, this has to stop.’ I was just kidding. That would be a tough one. But you never know in life, do you, in favor of transgender mutilazation, that’s these people that you’re thinking about maybe voting for.”
Okay, so not the clearest presidential oratory ever. But Trump did say twice that he was just “kidding” about renaming oceans.

But then later in his remarks on Thursday, he casually used his new name for New Mexico. “If you were on the Texas border, if you were in Arizona or if you were in New America,” he said, pausing for applause.

So was this another joke, or is Trump just going to start referring to New Mexico by a new name to see if it sticks? Who knows. But while discussing the renaming of Lake Ontario earlier this week, Trump did confirm one reason why he’s so determined to continue his stupid renaming spree.
“I did it very lightly and the damn thing got changed! That’s power, right? When you sort of do it half-heartedly and it gets changed!” Trump said. “So that’s very, very nice.”

Magic mushrooms can make colors appear more vivid, alter the sense of time, and send thoughts in unfamiliar directions.
The compound responsible for these effects is called psilocybin, but there's still a lot we don't understand about how it works.
Psilocybin is of interest to scientists because of its potential to help treat mental health conditions under controlled conditions.
One question that remains to be solved is whether women and men have different experiences when they take the drug.
Knowing what someone might experience is important for preparing them beforehand and supporting them during a session.

In a new preprint study that has not yet undergone peer review, researchers from Maastricht University in the Netherlands found that women reported feeling some effects more strongly than men, though not all of them.
"What surprised me most was that these differences were selective," Natasha Mason, who studies how drugs affect the brain and behavior, told ScienceAlert.
Mason and fellow Maastricht researcher Eline Haijen-Bongers led a team that combined results from two trials involving 40 women and 32 men.
All were healthy volunteers with previous experience of drugs that alter perception and thought, known as psychedelics.
The volunteers did not eat mushrooms. They took psilocybin made in a laboratory.
The first trial compared it with another manufactured drug that changes perception and mood, called 2C-B. Participants received both drugs and an inactive substance on separate days.
The second trial examined LSD, another laboratory-made psychedelic. It was also compared with an inactive substance, or placebo.
Neither the volunteers nor the researchers working directly with them knew which substance they were receiving.
Participants rated how they felt throughout the sessions and answered questions about their experiences afterward. Researchers also collected blood samples.

Because some of the volunteers participated in both the trials, the 72 participants contributed 94 active-drug sessions altogether. The team's analysis took into account that the data in both trials came from the same people.
When the results were compared, women reported feeling more strongly under the influence. They also described greater reductions in alertness and felt less able to control their thinking.

Several differences remained after the researchers accounted for age differences between women and men. The difference in feeling under the influence was most pronounced with psilocybin. Reduced alertness differed significantly with psilocybin and 2C-B, but not with LSD.
Tests of understanding and responding emotionally to other people found no significant sex differences.

One possible explanation was body weight. Each drug was given at a fixed dose regardless of participants' weight. Because women in the study generally weighed less, the same dose could potentially produce higher drug concentrations in their blood.
But the blood measurements did not show this. Neither peak drug concentrations nor overall exposure during the measured period differed significantly between women and men.

The researchers are therefore considering other possibilities, including hormones. These drugs affect a brain signaling system involving a chemical messenger called serotonin. Hormones such as estrogen can also influence how that system works.
A separate review by members of the same Maastricht team, published in Molecular Psychiatry, explores these possible connections.
"That said, we did not measure hormone levels or account for menstrual cycle phase in this study, so we cannot determine whether hormones contributed to the differences we observed," Mason explained.

As scientists investigate how psychedelics affect the brain, understanding that people may need different support could help shape future treatments. The findings first need to be tested in larger studies and in patients receiving treatment.

Neither trial was originally designed to investigate sex differences. The sample was small, and the analysis did not adjust for the greater chance of false-positive findings when making multiple comparisons.
"It would certainly be premature to conclude that women need lower doses of psychedelics, or that they respond better or worse to psychedelic therapy," Mason cautioned.
The study did not investigate long-term therapeutic benefits.
The findings are reported in a preprint paper available at bioRxiv.

After decades of building isolated, vendor-locked systems to run the Air Operations Centers that serve as the Air Force’s “combat brains,” the program office tasked with creating the next-generation AOC is working to fold those systems into a new cloud-based system.

Col. Brian Viola, the newly appointed commander of Kessel Run, the government-led, vendor-managed program office underneath the portfolio acquisition executive for command, control, communications, and battle management, told Air & Space Forces Magazine in a recent interview that his team is standardizing how cloud-based applications and software updates to AOCs get accessed worldwide in real time.

Starting this spring, Kessel Run launched the Dynamic Unified Net-enabled Environment, or DUNE, which merges cloud and on-premises capabilities for AOC operators, commanders, and their customers—the rest of the operational Air Force.

“Evolving the architectural foundation is vital because the information our warfighters rely on depends on the integrity, speed, and agility of the underlying domain,” Viola said. “We are rapidly entering the era of software-defined warfare, where tactical superiority belongs to the force that can iterate, secure and deploy code faster than the adversary can adapt.”
Essentially, DUNE standardizes how legacy and current software communicates across the Air Operations Center’s systems.

It’s unclear whether the DUNE acronym is a nod to the popular book, film and TV franchise of the same name. But the Air Force has a history of using sci-fi-inspired names and acronyms—Kessel Run itself is named after a Star Wars reference.
Currently, Viola said, AOC operators must choose between using real-time, cloud-based tools or sticking with the often aged, legacy hardware they have on hand.
“The ability to rapidly integrate new mission capabilities, enable distributed command and control, and incorporate new technologies depends on the architecture beneath them,” he said.

DUNE is an overarching project that builds on Kessel Run’s Applications Transformation project, or AppTX, which the service introduced to conduct large-scale migrations of legacy software apps to the cloud. Companies such as Parsons, General Dynamics Information Technology, and Astrion compete for taskings through AppTX.

DUNE focuses on the issue of Data Definition Language, which has gained prominence with the recent push to rush artificial intelligence into systems across the Pentagon. DDL is a kind of programming language that can create, modify, or delete database structures without modifying the data itself—it allows legacy infrastructure and software “talk” with new software and applications, breaking down silos and stovepipes.

Without it, Viola said, “you’re going to have to work with what you have”—an Airman in an AOC will only be able to draw from a tool or solution they have in their local network, on site near the tactical edge, without access to the cloud.

“We don’t want to necessarily have every AOC be a snowflake that we have to go, ‘this is tailored for you now, AOC 1, and this is tailored for the 613th [AOC], this is tailored for the 607th [AOC],” Viola said.
Tailoring the solutions by AOC is “sucking away from the innovation we really want to get after,” he said.
Project DUNE aims to get the continuous delivery of cloud-based capabilities and applications down to an on-premises solution, he said.
Solutions won’t be as “elastic” as the cloud, but they will be a resilient capability that users can rely on, he said.

Beyond DUNE, Viola said next steps include building the “Revolutionary AOC” with industry partners. The effort will involve operators, mission partners, engineers and acquisition teams working together in operational scenarios to identify gaps and improve the system architecture.

Work on DUNE and recent pushes in the PAE C3BM and Kessel Run specifically predate Viola’s tenure. Air & Space Forces Magazine reported in February that Kessel Run was launching its “next generation” AOC effort, which seeks to integrate AI, machine learning, data fusion, and cloud-based software into the centers.
The Air Force has 21 AOCs across the force and sees these operational hubs as weapons systems in their own right, calling them AN/USQ-163 Falconers.

In 2022, the Air Force awarded SAIC a $374 million contract through mid-2027 to sustain and modernize its AOCs. The current Falconer system is in Increment 10.1, with a 10.2 (aka Block 20) upgrade in progress.

Less than a week after an airman died from injuries sustained during a rappelling incident, the service member’s special operations unit has suspended all rappel and ropes training events and demonstrations.

On Saturday, Tech. Sgt. Ian Patterson, a Tactical Air Control Party instructor assigned to the 6th Combat Training Squadron, Detachment 2, at Joint Base San Antonio, Texas, fell from a football stadium’s rafters during a rappelling demonstration before a game between the University of Texas at San Antonio and the U.S. Naval Academy.

During UTSA’s annual Salute to Armed Forces & Veterans game, videos show Patterson wearing combat fatigues and rappelling down to midfield from the Alamodome’s rafters before falling onto the field at full speed, feet first. Subsequent videos show medical personnel assisting the airman on the field before transporting him to a local hospital.
Later Saturday night, Nellis Air Force Base, Nevada, which houses the 6th Combat Training Squadron, announced Patterson had died at the hospital from the injuries sustained during the demonstration.
Members of the 6th Combat Training Squadron are trained in rappelling from heights of 100 feet or more. The football stadium’s rafters are around 170 feet above the stadium floor.

“Tech Sgt Patterson’s squadron, 6th Combat Training Squadron, has paused all rappel and ropes training events and demonstrations until further notice,” an Air Force Warfare Center spokesperson told Military Times.
The spokesperson declined to comment on when the suspension began and who enacted it. The comment did not include when the office expects the events and demonstrations to continue.

Rappelling and ropes are a large aspect of the Tactical Air Control Party’s skill base, with familiarization training designed to give service members basic information and techniques needed to conduct live operations, according to an Air Force description.

Patterson was from Fort Stewart, Georgia, and served in the Air Force for 15 years. His decorations include the Air and Space Commendation Medal with three oak leaf clusters, as well as the Army Commendation Medal, Air and Space Achievement Medal and Army Achievement Medal, each with one oak leaf cluster.
He was named the Air Force Special Warfare Enlisted Instructor of the Year at the headquarters level in 2022.
The incident is currently under investigation, according to a release at the time of identification.

As NASA’s Curiosity rover recently began climbing up a Martian valley nicknamed “Valle Grande,” it sent back images that were a familiar sight to mission scientists: honeycomb-like textures called polygonal fractures, each one about 1.5 to 3 inches (4 to 8 centimeters) across. The mission has spotted small patches of these geometric shapes several times before, but nothing at the scale discovered in Valle Grande.

In a 360-degree panorama that the rover captured on June 19 and 20, the 4,930th and 4,931st Martian days, or sols, of the mission, the polygonal shapes spread in all directions for as far as the rover can see. They even wrap around the sides of a nearby butte nicknamed “Miraflores,” which stands 20 feet (6 meters) tall and is topped with a thick cap of sand.

“We’ve seen a lot of fascinating landscapes through Curiosity’s eyes, but this sea of polygons took our breath away,” said the mission’s project scientist, Ashwin Vasavada of NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Southern California. “We measured their shapes and chemistry carefully and are hopeful there are clues in the data as to how these features formed.”

Some of the polygons that the mission has spotted in the past clearly formed as mud cracks, though a variety of processes can contribute to their honeycomb textures, including cycles of warm and cold temperatures or compression that squeezed water out of the sediment when the surface was buried.

These newly discovered polygons are among the many surprises Curiosity has trundled across since landing on Mars 14 years ago, on Aug. 5, 2012. Besides sulfur crystals, shiny meteorites, and other interesting geologic features, the rover has made major discoveries about the ancient Martian environment — most importantly, that it had the water, chemistry, and nutrients to support microbial life.

Billions of years ago, lakes and streams dappled the lower foothills of Mount Sharp, a 3-mile-tall (5-kilometer-tall) mountain that Curiosity has been ascending since 2014. The rover has previously uncovered chemistry left over from Mars’ watery history, including carbon-based molecules believed to be precursors to RNA and DNA, two nucleic acids that carry genetic information. Scientists have no way of knowing whether these organic molecules were created by biologic or geologic processes — either path is possible — but their discovery reconfirmed that ancient Mars had the right chemistry to support life.
Managed by Caltech in Pasadena, JPL built Curiosity and leads the mission on behalf of NASA’s Science Mission Directorate in Washington as part of the agency’s Mars Exploration Program portfolio.
NASA is helping to foster long-term energy security in Virginia.

NASA’s Langley Research Center in Hampton, Virginia, is partnering with the Virginia Department of Energy to support informed decisions for effective energy generation, delivery and use by providing solar, meteorological, and future weather risk datasets for energy system modeling and planning purposes.

Under a new Space Act Agreement announced during a ceremony Friday, the partnership will use NASA expertise in atmospheric sciences to assist Virginia Energy in support of resiliency studies, resource analysis, and long-term energy planning.

“NASA Langley relishes the opportunity to put our unique science data into the hands of those who want to improve people’s lives,” said NASA Langley Deputy Director Allen Kilgore. “This collaboration with Virginia Energy will benefit the citizens of Virginia and provide stronger energy security for the Commonwealth.”

This agreement will help state officials plan for current and potential extreme weather conditions in Virginia and assess implications for electricity demand, energy generation, and system stress. Information can be directly incorporated into energy policy, planning, and operational decisions.

By helping Virginians better anticipate energy demands, prepare for extreme weather, and understand factors affecting electricity generation, this partnership will support a more reliable and resilient energy system.

“Sound energy planning depends on models that reflect real-world conditions,” said Virginia Energy Director Vince Maiden. “This collaboration will help us better understand how weather affects electricity supply and demand, identify vulnerabilities, and weigh resource tradeoffs with greater confidence.”

The partnership will infuse relevant NASA Prediction of Worldwide Energy Resources (POWER) data products into Virginia Energy’s modeling and analysis system. The POWER information supports energy generation system designs and prediction of energy production using validated data products from NASA’s Earth Science to Action program. Those key NASA products represent research and development across NASA including Langley, Goddard Space Flight Center in Greenbelt, Maryland, and Ames Research Center in California’s Silicon Valley.

Through a digital pipeline, Virginia Energy can connect to Langley’s POWER web platform to download specific datasets and put them directly into their modeling tools. NASA’s POWER team members will work with Virginia Energy researchers to streamline the exchange, adjust formats, and evaluate the need for additional data.

This new partnership was fostered through NASA Langley’s Strategic Partnerships Office that connects industry, academia, and other government agencies with center facilities, capabilities, specialized test environments, and technical expertise to bring ideas to life.

PARIS — France and the United Kingdom carried out a joint airborne nuclear strike exercise for the first time, with Eurofighter Typhoon jets from the Royal Air Force escorting French Rafale jets on a simulated nuclear-strike mission.

The French and British fighter jets flew a joint mission on Tuesday during the exercise Rummy, the French Armed Forces Ministry said in a statement on Friday, calling the drill a show of growing cooperation in the framework of an agreement last year for closer nuclear cooperation and coordination between the two countries.

France is working with several European allies on a concept of “forward deterrence” amid uncertainty around United States security guarantees for Europe in the face of an aggressive Russia. While both France and the U.K. operate strategic ballistic-missile submarines as a nuclear deterrent, France has an airborne component, which the U.K. lacks, in the shape of Rafale jets carrying nuclear-tipped cruise missiles.

“Having independent nuclear forces doesn’t exclude coordination,” French Armed Forces Minister Catherine Vautrin said. “By coordinating, our nuclear forces demonstrate that they can contribute even more significantly to the overall security of the alliance and the peace and stability of the Euro-Atlantic zone.”

The British aircraft operated alongside those of France’s Strategic Air Forces over the Mediterranean, with Typhoons escorting Rafale fighters, according to the ministry. While the Rafale jets performed a simulated nuclear strike, the exercise didn’t involve any actual nuclear weapons, the ministry said.

In addition to Eurofighter Typhoon and Rafale jets, the exercise included A330 MRTT tanker aircraft, French Armed Forces Chief of Staff Gen. Fabien Mandon said in a post on the social network X. The French and British crews took off from Saint-Dizier air base in northeastern France, and showed a “very high level of interoperability and a capability to coordinate,” he said.
Mandon’s post included a picture showing three taxiing Eurofighters, as well as a Eurofighter under a hard cover with the markings of the RAF 29 Squadron.

“This is a revolution for the Strategic Air Forces, which have always operated in complete autonomy since their creation in the 1960s,” said Etienne Marcuz, a senior analyst at the Fondation pour la Recherche Stratégique, in a post on X. He called the involvement of at least three British Eurofighter aircraft “quite significant.”

The exercise was an important step in the implementation of the Northwood Declaration, showing a determination to deter common threats together, the ministry said. France and the U.K. last year agreed to deepen nuclear cooperation and coordination, stating in the declaration that they agreed there was no extreme threat to Europe that would not prompt a response by both nations.
The exercise Rummy took place on Oct. 20 and 21, according to the ministry. France’s Air and Space Force regularly holds simulated nuclear-strike exercises called Poker.

The U.K. and France maintain sovereign and independent nuclear forces, and decision-making regarding their use isn’t shared, the ministry said. The countries would only consider using nuclear weapons in “extreme circumstances of legitimate defense,” the French ministry said.

In nearly a century of Oscars, not a single documentary has been nominated for best picture. But that shouldn’t be the case.

While a documentary can win its own Oscar, reshape the cultural conversation and become one of the defining films of its era, these nonfiction feature films have been excluded from the top category meant to honor the year’s best filmmaking. When the Academy expanded the Best Picture lineup from five to 10 after the snub of “The Dark Knight” (2008), the press release led with the possibility of a documentary getting recognized. That has yet to happen … perhaps until now?

That assumption is finally being tested this season with “You Can See Everything,” Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s nonfiction sensation about Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes. Acclaim and box office success are raising the possibility that a documentary could finally break one of the Academy’s longest-standing barriers. If it earns a nomination, the achievement would be historic. But it would also raise an uncomfortable question: Why did it take this long?
To celebrate this potential historic nomination, Variety is ranking the 20 films that should have received a best picture nomination in the past 40 years.

The films mentioned here span genres, styles and subjects, from the pursuit of an NBA dream to a high-wire walk between the World Trade Center towers, from a confrontation with Indonesia’s history of mass killing to a real-time account of Edward Snowden’s revelations.
You can blame the Academy at large for some of these omissions; others tie directly to the Documentary Branch itself, which snubbed many of them in its own category.

If “You Can See Everything” finally breaks through, it will undoubtedly have earned its place in history. But it should not have been the first. Many others from this very year could also be deemed worthy, such as “Once Upon a Time in Harlem” and “Naza.”
Honorable mentions: “An Inconvenient Truth” (2006); “Senna” (2010); “The Act of Killing” (2012); “Apollo 11″ (2019)

Daughters (2024)Angela Patton and Natalie Rae’s “Daughters” follows four girls preparing for a father-daughter dance inside a Washington, D.C., prison as part of a fatherhood program Patton helped build. The filmmakers’ choice to focus on the girls’ anticipation, anger and longing is its strongest element. It carries the film toward a dance sequence of almost unbearable tenderness. It won both the Audience Award and the Festival Favorite prize at Sundance, then made the documentary shortlist only to miss the nomination at the 2025 ceremony. Few films that year said more about love under impossible conditions.

Man on Wire (2008)James Marsh’s “Man on Wire” reconstructs Philippe Petit’s 1974 high-wire walk between the World Trade Center towers. Through interviews, archival footage and recreations, Marsh builds a structure as a model for any good movie heist. “Man on Wire” won the documentary Oscar at the 2009 ceremony, and its success lives on, demonstrating how effectively a nonfiction film could deliver the pleasures of a caper.

O.J.: Made in America (2016)There are strong feelings about whether or not Ezra Edelman’s Oscar winner is, in fact, a documentary feature, but it’s included nonetheless. Edelman’s nearly eight-hour “O.J.: Made in America” is an expansive examination of race, celebrity, policing and the American justice system, using the life of O.J. Simpson as a lens through which to understand the country’s social and cultural divisions. What begins as a portrait of an athlete becomes a sweeping account of Los Angeles and the forces that shaped one of the most consequential public dramas of the modern era. The documentary feature Oscar winner’s format also exposed the boundaries of the category. Its recognition prompted renewed scrutiny of how the Academy treats multipart nonfiction projects, contributing to subsequent eligibility changes concerning episodic work. Whatever the debate over its classification, the filmmaking is extraordinary. Its scope exceeds that of most narrative features.

Won’t You Be My Neighbor? (2018)Morgan Neville’s portrait of television icon Fred Rogers became the highest-grossing biographical documentary of its time and became a sensation for all of us who grew up with the prolific figure. Rather than canonize its subject, Oscar winner Neville (“20 Feet From Stardom”) examines the radical patience behind “Mister Rogers’ Neighborhood” and the quiet conviction that children deserved to be taken seriously. The film made the documentary shortlist but, shockingly, missed a nomination at the 2019 ceremony, a snub that still stings. Few films that year moved audiences so completely, in any category.

Flee (2021)Jonas Poher Rasmussen’s “Flee” uses animation to tell the story of Amin, an Afghan refugee who reveals the full extent of his childhood and his journey to safety. The decision to use the animation medium for the testimony allows Amin to revisit traumatic memories while preserving his anonymity, creating a visual language for experiences that would be difficult to reconstruct. “Flee” made Oscar history by becoming the first film nominated for documentary feature, international feature and animated feature in the same year. It lost in all three categories, and best picture remained out of reach. Rasmussen’s film is a reminder that nonfiction is not confined to one visual language or storytelling tradition.

The Look of Silence (2014)Many will argue I chose the wrong Joshua Oppenheimer film, and that “The Act of Killing” is more worthy of a spot than its companion piece. That a filmmaker’s work can spark such a debate is itself a mark of genius. “The Look of Silence” approaches Indonesia’s 1965-66 mass killings through an optometrist whose brother was murdered during the violence. Oppenheimer resists the conventions of a historical exposé, allowing pauses and glances to communicate what his subjects refuse to say. The film landed a documentary feature nomination but lost to “Amy.”

Cameraperson (2016)Kirsten Johnson spent decades as a documentary cinematographer, filming subjects in war zones, hospitals and interview rooms. With “Cameraperson,” she assembled fragments from that career into a moving essay about the ethics of looking and the emotional toll of bearing witness. The doc branch failed to nominate “Cameraperson,” a shocking omission for a work so widely admired for its originality. Johnson’s 2020 follow-up, “Dick Johnson Is Dead,” a playful and heartbreaking reckoning with her father’s decline, that could just as easily have claimed this spot.

13th (2016)Ava DuVernay’s “13th” examines the connection between the 13th Amendment, which abolished slavery, and the rise of mass incarceration in the United States. Through interviews with scholars, activists and politicians, alongside archival footage, DuVernay builds an argument about the enduring relationship between race and the criminal justice system. Rather than treating the amendment as a historical endpoint, she traces how its language became a blueprint for systems of control, and presenting a complex history with clarity and urgency. “13th” opened the 2016 New York Film Festival and landed a documentary feature nom, losing to “O.J.: Made in America.” A decade later, DuVernay returned to NYFF with the equally urgent “14th,” the festival’s 2026 closing night film, which Netflix will also release.

Dear Zachary: A Letter to a Son About His Father (2008)No documentary has made me cry more than the one about a baby named Zachary. Kurt Kuenne began “Dear Zachary” as a film for the infant son of his murdered best friend, Andrew Bagby. And what starts as a tribute built from home videos, photographs and memories becomes a devastating account of grief, family and a legal system that fails those seeking justice. Kuenne is not a detached observer. As events unfold, the film’s purpose changes, and its structure takes on a force no viewer can anticipate. Kuenne’s mid-film narration is something your heart can never properly prepare for. Nonetheless, the documentary branch passed on “Dear Zachary.” It remains one of the clearest examples of why documentaries deserve to be considered among the year’s best films, not merely the year’s best documentaries.

Exit Through the Gift Shop (2010)Banksy’s “Exit Through the Gift Shop” makes uncertainty part of the moviewatching experience. Is the film documenting an absurd art-world spectacle, manufacturing one or doing both at once? Banksy never provides a definitive answer, and the film’s refusal to settle the question gives it life. “Exit Through the Gift Shop” earned a documentary feature nom, losing to “Inside Job.” Moreover, it challenged the assumption that documentaries must present a distinction between observer and participant.

I Am Not Your Negro (2016)Raoul Peck’s Oscar-nominated “I Am Not Your Negro” takes James Baldwin’s unfinished manuscript about Medgar Evers, Malcolm X and Martin Luther King Jr. and transforms it into a searing cinematic essay on race and America. Samuel L. Jackson narrates Baldwin’s words, with the film’s force coming from the collision between the writer’s observations and a country that still refuses to reckon with its past. It’s sheer brilliance, and always timely.

Three Identical Strangers (2018)Tim Wardle’s film opens as a feel-good reunion of triplets separated at birth and curdles into an account of a secret psychological study that treated infants as test subjects. Wardle controls the revelations with the discipline of a thriller, letting each turn leave the viewer shocked before the next is revealed. Like “Won’t You Be My Neighbor?,” it was shortlisted and then passed over entirely by the documentary branch. Its story of nature, nurture and institutional betrayal deserved a much wider stage.

Citizenfour (2014)Laura Poitras’ “Citizenfour” puts viewers inside a Hong Kong hotel room while Edward Snowden meets journalists and begins revealing classified information about government surveillance. Poitras allows conversations to develop in real time, building suspense through the simple act of watching history unfold. “Citizenfour” won the documentary Oscar at the 2015 ceremony, but no best picture heat would ensue.

Searching for Sugar Man (2012)Malik Bendjelloul’s “Searching for Sugar Man” chases the ghost of Rodriguez, a Detroit musician whose albums vanished in America but became anthems in apartheid-era South Africa, where fans knew nothing about the man behind the music. By my estimation, it’s the single standout nonfiction film of its decade. Bendjelloul builds the mystery like a detective story, with an emotional payoff that feels almost too extraordinary to be true. Rodriguez’s incredible songs carry a story about fame, obscurity and the strange ways art outlives the circumstances of its making. Oscar voters handed it the documentary prize in 2013. Nobody mounted a best picture push for a film that had already proven it could hold a broad audience in its palm. Bendjelloul died in 2014 at 36, but the joyous discovery he left behind is well intact.

Grizzly Man (2005)Werner Herzog’s “Grizzly Man” begins with footage shot by Timothy Treadwell, a self-appointed protector of Alaskan grizzlies who was killed by one of the animals he sought to defend. Herzog’s narration becomes a film unto itself, challenging Treadwell’s romantic vision of the wilderness. The footage is funny, unnerving and devastating, sometimes within the same frame. Few filmmakers have turned a real-life tragedy into a philosophical inquiry so effectively without losing sight of the person at its center. Unfortunately, this was yet another victim of the doc branch’s allergy to mainstream and successful films, even though it’s widely considered among Herzog’s most celebrated works.

Stories We Tell (2012)Sarah Polley’s “Stories We Tell” is an investigation into her own family history and becomes a remarkably intricate exploration of memory, and the fragile relationship between personal truth and the stories people preserve. Polley interviews relatives and friends, reconstructing family moments with its most effective moments being best experienced without advance knowledge of the revelations it shows. “Stories We Tell” was snubbed for the documentary Oscar, let alone best picture. That omission is particularly striking given Polley’s command of structure and her willingness to question the very conventions on which documentary filmmaking depends.

Bowling for Columbine (2002)Michael Moore turned the Columbine High School massacre into a mirror for America to see. “Bowling for Columbine” interrogates America’s relationship with guns, violence and fear, mixing interviews, archival footage and Moore’s confrontational on-camera presence into an argument that dared audiences to fight back. Few releases of 2002 commanded that attention. The Writers Guild made it the first documentary to win its original screenplay prize, and the Academy followed with the documentary Oscar, where Moore’s “shame on you, Mr. Bush” speech became the most talked-about moment of the night (and history).

Hoop Dreams (1994)No documentary snub remains quite as painful as the Academy’s failure to recognize Steve James’ “Hoop Dreams.” Over five years, James followed Chicago teenagers William Gates and Arthur Agee as they pursued basketball dreams that promised an escape from poverty. The result is a nearly three-hour American epic about race, class, family and the machinery that turns young athletes into commodities. Critics embraced the film as one of the year’s finest, regardless of genre. The Academy’s documentary branch, however, failed to nominate it, prompting widespread criticism and contributing to voting changes in the documentary nomination process. Interestingly, “Hoop Dreams” managed to receive an Oscar nomination for film editing, but best picture was likely an even more distant possibility.

The Thin Blue Line (1988)Errol Morris’ investigation into the 1976 killing of a Dallas police officer did something few doc films hope to do: It helped free an innocent man. Randall Dale Adams was released from prison within a year of the film’s debut, after Morris’ interviews exposed the holes in the case against him. Its stylized reenactments, Philip Glass score and noir structure reinvented the nonfiction form in many ways. Once again, the doc branch had other plans, with a snub measured just as scandalous in its moment as “Hoop Dreams” would be six years later. Leaving out the film that changed how documentaries are made is indefensible.

Paris is Burning (1990)Jennie Livingston’s “Paris Is Burning” documents Harlem’s ballroom scene in the late 1980s, where Black and Latino queer performers built houses, families and an entire vocabulary of survival in the face of poverty, racism and the AIDS crisis. Its subjects, including Pepper LaBeija, Dorian Corey and Venus Xtravaganza, are among the most vivid figures nonfiction cinema has captured. The film won the Grand Jury Prize at Sundance yet was snubbed by the Academy’s documentary branch at the 1992 ceremony. Decades later, its influence has been felt in artistic achievements such as television’s “Pose,” “RuPaul’s Drag Race” and the mainstream itself.
New evidence suggests spinosaurus spent most of its life underwater

- Millions of years after animals first conquered land, some took an extraordinary evolutionary U-turn and returned to the water. Using machine learning and thousands of fossil measurements, Yale scientists have uncovered surprising clues about which prehistoric creatures truly became aquatic. Their findings suggest that Spinosaurus spent most of its life underwater, while some ancient marine reptiles previously thought to be fully aquatic actually spent considerable time on land.

For millions of years, evolution helped animals make the transition from life in the ocean to life on land. But the journey did not always move in one direction. Many species eventually returned to the water, developing new adaptations that allowed them to thrive in aquatic environments.

Dozens of major groups of mammals and reptiles made this remarkable evolutionary reversal. Now, a new study from Yale University is shedding light on when and how these transitions occurred, as well as which ancient animals became fully aquatic and which continued to depend on land.
The findings were published in the journal Current Biology.

"These secondarily aquatic groups adapted in strikingly similar ways to their new aquatic home -- evolving flippers and a suite of other features that made them better swimmers," said lead author Caleb Gordon, who completed his doctorate at Yale's Graduate School of Arts and Sciences (GSAS) earlier this year and is now a postdoctoral researcher at the Florida Museum of Natural History. "As a result, they've become textbook examples of convergent evolution, which can tell us a lot about the processes driving and constraining adaptive change in response to similar environmental cues."
Using Ancient Fossils and AI to Reconstruct Evolution

To investigate these evolutionary changes, the researchers examined hundreds of fossil and modern specimens housed at the Yale Peabody Museum and dozens of other institutions worldwide. They collected extensive new data, including measurements (more than 11,000), photographs, and CT scans.

The team combined traditional paleontological techniques with machine learning models that account for evolutionary relationships. They also incorporated a statistical approach originally used by naval forces during World War II. Together, these methods offered a new way to investigate one of the most remarkable transitions in vertebrate evolution.

"Reconstructing the lives of extinct life forms in a scientifically rigorous way, as opposed to just telling stories, is a precise and delicate undertaking," said Bhart-Anjan Bhullar, senior author of the study. Bhullar is an associate professor of Earth and planetary sciences in Yale's Faculty of Arts and Sciences (FAS) and an associate curator of vertebrate paleontology and vertebrate zoology at the Peabody Museum.

"It requires a careful interweaving of data from modern organisms, of which our understanding is necessarily far deeper, and knowledge of these living organisms' genealogy relative to fossil forms," he said. "Caleb's work accomplishes all of this and more, and on a massive evolutionary scale."

For decades, scientists have disagreed about when particular groups of prehistoric animals became fully adapted to life underwater. The fossil record often provides incomplete or conflicting clues, making it difficult to determine whether an extinct species primarily lived on land, in water, or in both environments.

Some skeletal features may indicate an aquatic lifestyle, while others suggest that the same animal remained capable of moving and feeding on land. These contradictions have led researchers to different conclusions about how ancient species behaved.
"In these cases, paleontologists are often stuck, as different lines of evidence disagree about what the ancient animal was like," Gordon said.

To address this uncertainty, Gordon developed a method using relatively simple but effective machine learning models trained on living animals. By identifying relationships between skeletal proportions and known lifestyles, the models can estimate how extinct species used aquatic environments. They can also predict soft tissue adaptations, including swimming structures that rarely survive in fossils.
Spinosaurus May Have Spent Most of Its Life Underwater
One of the most striking findings concerns Spinosaurus, a giant prehistoric dinosaur whose relationship with water has generated considerable controversy.

Spinosaurus lived approximately 113 million to 94 million years ago in what is now northern Africa. Although scientists generally agree that it was associated with aquatic environments, exactly how it moved, hunted, and spent its time remains a subject of debate.

Some evidence points to an animal that frequently submerged itself and pursued prey underwater, much like seals or penguins. Other findings suggest a lifestyle closer to that of a modern heron, with Spinosaurus walking and searching for food along shorelines and in shallow water.
The Yale team's analysis provides new support for the more aquatic interpretation.

"Our results shed new light on how much time Spinosaurus spent submerged, which could support the underwater hunting view," Gordon said. "We confidently recovered highly aquatic habits for Spinosaurus, indicating that it spent the vast majority of its time submerged in the water."
Although the findings do not settle every question about how Spinosaurus hunted, they strengthen the case that this enormous predator spent much more of its life underwater than on land.
Ancient Marine Reptiles That Never Fully Left Land

The researchers reached a different conclusion about mesosaurs, small marine reptiles that lived between 290 million and 274 million years ago in regions now forming parts of South Africa and eastern South America.

Mesosaurs have long interested paleontologists because they gave birth to live young, a characteristic some researchers have interpreted as evidence of a fully aquatic existence. However, the new analysis suggests that their limbs were not adapted for a life spent entirely in water.
Instead, their skeletal proportions indicate that mesosaurs regularly moved between aquatic and terrestrial environments.
"They spent a lot of time on land, like a modern-day alligator or platypus does," Gordon said. "Mesosaurs didn't completely leave the land behind."

The findings also suggest a broader pattern among the earliest marine reptiles. According to the researchers, all Paleozoic marine reptiles (all marine reptiles around before the dinosaurs appeared) continued to return to land regularly. None appeared to have evolved a completely aquatic lifestyle, with even the most water adapted species remaining amphibious.

The researchers found that forelimb proportions were particularly useful for distinguishing these lifestyles. Using this information, their models could predict with more than 90% accuracy whether an animal possessed soft tissue flippers and whether it had highly or fully aquatic habits.
A World War II Technique Helps Solve an Evolutionary Mystery
An especially unusual part of the research involved adapting a statistical method developed during the 1940s.

"Caleb resurrected a statistical technique from a bygone era," said co-author Jacques Gauthier, a professor of Earth and planetary sciences at Yale and curator-in-charge for vertebrate paleontology at the Peabody Museum. "It was developed during WWII to estimate the probability that an approaching blip on the radar screen was an enemy plane. Caleb cleverly used it to get at whether or not an extinct animal had limbs modified for swimming."
By repurposing this approach, the researchers could assess the likelihood that an extinct species possessed specialized swimming adaptations, even when direct evidence of those features was missing.

The method could eventually help scientists investigate other major changes in evolutionary history. Potential applications include studying when human ancestors developed the ability to walk on two legs and how the dinosaur ancestors of birds evolved the ability to fly.

Because most prehistoric vertebrates are known primarily through their fossilized skeletons, reconstructing their behavior is one of paleontology's greatest challenges. Bones preserve valuable information, but they rarely provide a complete picture of how an animal lived.

Traditionally, scientists have interpreted particular skeletal features to make arguments about the lifestyles of extinct species. Those interpretations can differ significantly, especially when fossils are incomplete or several anatomical characteristics point toward different conclusions.
The new approach offers a more systematic way to evaluate that evidence, using patterns observed in living species to make testable predictions about animals that disappeared millions of years ago.

"Bones are all that is left to us of the vast majority of vertebrate animals that have lived on Earth," Bhullar said. "We want to know so very much about these creatures and the succession of lost worlds they inhabited, but we have so little on which to base our conclusions. From skeletal remains, people have tried to discern life habits, generally making an argument on the basis of one preferred set of features or another. Caleb's method removes the subjectivity from this process and allows the data to speak for themselves."

The study's additional co-authors are Lisa Freisem, a doctoral student at Yale's Graduate School of Arts and Sciences, and Christopher Griffin, an assistant professor of geosciences at Princeton University who previously worked as a postdoctoral fellow at Yale.

Mary Robertson hopes Matthew Perry would think her Netflix documentary about him is funny. “I think Matthew would be really upset if I made a film about his life that wasn’t funny,” she says. “It was very important to me that this film be as funny as it could be, and that we find levity in the darkness and in the sorrowful moments. I don’t think that humor diminishes our grief, or our understanding of his struggles.” The One About Matthew Perry, a three-part docuseries, out October 27 on Netflix, is more of a celebration of celebrate Perry’s life instead of a mournful tribute or true crime drama about his death and the headline-making trial that followed. Robertson traces Perry’s life as a child of divorce to a hopeful comedic actor to star of one of the biggest TV shows of all time.

The series interviews two of Perry’s closest friends — industry pal Kevin Pollak, and his sister Mia Perry Bowick, who eventually became a therapist well-versed in addiction in large part because of her big brother’s struggle. “Mia has a line in the film that I adore,” Robertson says. “‘Our job is not to make the feeling go away, but to allow them to sit in the feeling.’ I think about that line every single day of my life now. I try to bring that spirit and idea into my practice as a documentary filmmaker.”

Like hundreds of millions, I am a Matthew Perry fan. I grew up watching Friends. I’m of the age that I grew up watching it as appointment viewing on NBC on Thursdays, when it was part of the monoculture. I remember feeling a deep attachment to the show, but specifically to Matthew and to the sense of warmth and comfort that his performance of Chandler evoked. I think about that word comfort a lot these days because now that I’m able to talk about the film, I hear other people share their stories about appreciating Matthew and so many of them talk about this sense of comfort that they got from Chandler Bing’s character, which I think is pretty interesting, given that the character had these sharp edges at times. He was a sarcastic character, but Matthew infused it with human vulnerability, which fostered this sense of attachment.

When his memoir came out, I read it very quickly. I was moved by his candor and his humor. He begins the book by saying “I should be dead,” and signals almost immediately that he’s not going to hold anything back. After reading the book, I wrote to several folks who were affiliated with its publication, didn’t hear anything back, but never forgot about the power of his words. He was willing to speak openly about being a huge celebrity and struggling with addiction over decades and decades.

After Matthew passed, I was deeply saddened, but remained interested in excavating the full story of Matthew. It was not immediately in the wake of his passing, but months later, my team and I felt ready to start doing outreach. We wrote some letters and sent some DMs to people close to Matthew. This time was clearly different. I think there was a sense at this moment that, perhaps, some of the people who were close to Matthew were ready. They wanted to shift the focus away from his death and back onto how he lived.
We pitched the project to Netflix. They understood immediately that this could and should be a film that was loving, and rendered Matthew in a fulsome manner.

We wrote a letter to Mia Perry Bowick, Matthew’s sister, hoping that she would respond. We were skeptical that we would get a response, given that she likely received hundreds of such missives over the decades. Mia did respond. I screamed when her email landed in my inbox and she asked to set up a Zoom. I remember when she hopped on, her wonderful husband David was sitting next to her, and they looked at each other. And they inhaled and exhaled and then looked at me and my colleagues and said, “We’re nervous.” And we inhaled and exhaled and said, “We’re nervous, too.”

Mia’s therapy experience brings so much to the documentary. There’s the same uncomfortable silence in interviews as there are therapy sessions How has doing this project affected your relationship with discomfort and with silences?

That is the best question I’ve ever been asked. I’ve been working in documentary film for over 25 years. The longer I work in it, the more I want my practice to align with the practice of a good therapist. I am not a trained therapist, but I do think that it is of value to give the people who are so generously sharing their stories and their time with me space to sit in their feelings.

Mia has a line in the film that I adore. “Our job is not to make the feeling go away, but to allow them to sit in the feeling.” I think about that line every single day of my life now. I try to bring that spirit and idea into my practice as a documentary filmmaker. What this means, specifically, is not interrupting people and fostering an environment where the person who’s on the other end of the conversation feels as though they can own the space fully and share all that they want to share.
The great tragedy of Perry’s life, I think, is the gulf between the tidy recovery narrative and the messy, everyday business of staying sober.

I think if Matthew were here today, he would want me to make clear that he saw addiction or substance-use disorder not as a failure of willpower, not as the result of a single circumstance or a collection of circumstances, but as a disease. There’s a clip that we include in the film that has previously gone viral where Matthew confronts Peter Hitchens. In essence, Hitchens tells Matthew that addiction is a failure of willpower and Matthew very forcefully responds that it is a disease, and that the science supports him in this understanding. I think if we hold on to that understanding too, then it’s a lot easier for us to understand why it’s so hard to beat.
Watching this series, you really understand how much Perry wanted to help people. Do you hope this documentary helps people in the same way?

I really hope this documentary helps people. It’s our intention that it helps people. It’s my intention that the film provide balm and entertainment, which is part of how we help people too. I think Matthew would be really upset if I made a film about his life that wasn’t funny. It was very important to me that this film be as funny as it could be, and that we find levity in the darkness and in the sorrowful moments. I don’t think that humor diminishes our grief, or our understanding of his struggles.

When it comes to what I want people to take away, beyond the sense of joy that Matthew wanted to impart to the world, I hope that people understand the size of the monster that was sitting on Matthew’s shoulders. And I hope that through Mia’s incredibly raw, brave testimony, the film is able to provide understanding and hopefully solace to everyone who’s living through an experience that’s similar to hers or similar to her brothers. I would venture to say that almost all of us have loved someone who has struggled with addiction.
Speaking of those moments of levity, I was surprised to learn so much about his music taste. You include at least one track that was important to him in every episode.
I was totally surprised to learn in the course of making this film that Matthew loved Enya, John Tesh, and “Drops of Jupiter.”
Were there any other tidbits about Matthew’s favorite things that didn’t make it into the doc?

Matthew loved Nestle Quick, I believe. He loved Batman. He loved macaroni and cheese. We do touch on his attachment to Batman in the film, and I think there’s a way in which we can understand Matthew’s life as having some parallels to Batman. There’s ways in which he was incredibly human, and then there’s ways in which he was extraordinarily impactful in the ways that superheroes are. There’s no question that he saved lives. We feature the account of one such person in our film, Tim Harrington, who attributes Matthew directly with saving his life.
Do you have a favorite Friends episode, and do you have a favorite Matthew Perry performance that’s not from Friends?

I think Matthew’s performance in Fools Rush In is really tender. He was pushing himself to exhibit his dramatic range. He’s a romantic lead. There’s vulnerability there that you see in Chandler’s character, but it’s expressed in a deeper way. I’m excited that we were able to include the account of Doug Draizin, who produced the film and was the character upon whom Matthew’s character was based.

Favorite Friends episode…it’s hard. We do feature in the documentary, [“The One With the Blackout”], where Matthew is stuck in the ATM booth with the supermodel Jill Goodacre. It is an incredible performance because Matthew is not speaking. There’s his internal monologue that you hear, but there’s so much of what is communicated is through his physicality. When his internal monologue does come in, it gives you this sense of his deeply held anxieties. He’s playing Chandler Bing at that point in time, but we feature one of the writers from Friends who said that they understood that they were also writing something for Matthew. There was a connection in that scene between what Matthew knew and felt and what Chandler they knew and felt.

I was recently watching a clip of Monica and Chandler posing for engagement photos. The whole joke is that Chandler is really bad at posing for photos. You could write that on the page, and if you asked me to then act that out, it wouldn’t be funny. No one would laugh. But his series of expressions and poses are just riotously funny.
Is it hard to rewatch Fools Rush In, knowing about the jet ski accident that took place on that set introduced him to opiates?

I don’t think it’s hard to watch Fools Rush In, and I think it’s a wonderful performance. Matthew was proud of it. His father in the film is played by his real-life father. Matthew’s relationship with his father was really touching in real life, and I know that working on the movie together was something that they both really savored. I see all the joy and the success, and the yearning and accomplishment, when I look at that film.

I was completely blown away by how relentlessly funny Matthew was in every public appearance. I mean, it is, it is a real gift. Spending time with Matthew through the film and with his friends did nothing, if not desperately make me want to be funnier. Still working on it.
